title: Slice-and-Serve: token-window reclamation + incremental model downgrades for OOM resilience
creator: Priya Shah
description:
Problem: Intermittent OOMs observed on p4d pools during sustained streaming workloads with wide token variance. Current responses are coarse-grained (full KV eviction, hard throttles, or model swap) and increase tail latency or produce failed responses for customers. Goal: introduce a low-latency, incremental OOM mitigation strategy that reclaims memory at token-window granularity and provides smooth, observable degradation paths (retries, partial outputs, model downgrades) rather than hard failures.

Scope: implement a Slice-and-Serve controller that operates at request admission time and during continuous batching. The controller will: (1) compute per-request token windows and soft-reclaim targets, (2) perform age-aware micro-evictions on KV segments (granular segment trimming rather than whole-key eviction), (3) apply incremental model downgrades (e.g., same-arch 8-bit micro-variants or distilled short-context variants) when reclaim budget is insufficient, and (4) orchestrate deterministic retry/backoff semantics with client-facing signals (retry-after, partial-response flags). This ticket covers design, prototype, unit+integration tests, and a limited canary rollout on dedicated staging pool.

Non-Goals: replacing global admission controllers, large refactors of batching engine, or introducing new public API fields in this phase. We will use existing SDK semantics for stream continuation and function-calling; where we add new response flags they will be internal first and productized later.
acceptance_criteria: End-to-end prototype on staging reduces gross OOM rate by >=70% for target workload (long streaming chat with 1–3k token prefixes) compared to baseline
When reclamation budget reached, controller either delivers a partial response with clear client signal or falls back to a pre-approved micro-model variant; no silent failures
Telemetry: add per-request reclaim_amount_bytes, eviction_segments_count, model_swap_reason to traces and dashboards; dashboards populated pre-rollout
Unit and integration tests covering token-window slice logic, KV micro-evict, and deterministic model downgrade path are present and green in CI
design_notes:
Key ideas: 1) Token-window reclamation: compute a sliding window over recent KV entries keyed by layer+sequence-range. Instead of evicting entire contexts, evict oldest sequence ranges in 128-token slabs with affinity-aware selection (hot token prefixes pinned). 2) Soft micro-eviction: mark segments as reclaimed and lazily free GPU buffers at safe scheduling points to avoid synchronous OOM spikes. 3) Probabilistic early-sampling: for large batches, sample membership to predict hotness and avoid evicting slabs belonging to highly reused prefixes. 4) Incremental model downgrade chain: runtime will consult an ordered list of compatible micro-variants (quantized/distilled) with known compatibility for KV formats; fallback happens deterministically based on reclaim shortfall and estimated latency trade-off. 5) Client signals: propagate structured flags in internal streaming envelope: partial=true|false, fallback_model=identifier, suggested_retry_ms. 6) Admission hook: budget-aware admission controller computes reclaim target per request and decides between soft reclaim vs. immediate fallback.

Trade-offs considered: eager slab eviction reduces memory quickly but may increase token recomputation and CPU bandwidth; lazy buffer free smooths out pressure but delays actual memory availability; model downgrades preserve progress at cost of fidelity and slightly different tokenization/outputs. We accept small fidelity regressions for heavy-memory emergency cases and will measure customer impact via eval prompts.
implementation_plan: Week 1: API+trace additions and design doc; add reclaim_amount_bytes and eviction_segments_count to trace schema; review with runtime leads
Week 2: Implement token-window slicer and slab allocator simulation in Python; unit tests for edge cases (very short prefixes, repeated prefixes)
Week 3: Implement soft micro-evict path in C++ runtime; ensure freed tensors are queued for safe free points; add metrics export
Week 4: Implement model-downgrade orchestrator (lookup + compatibility check); integrate with admission hook; add deterministic selection of fallback chain
Week 5: Integration tests with continuous-batching harness; synthetic stress tests to reproduce prior OOMs; iterate on thresholds
Week 6: Canary rollout to staging GPU pool, monitor dashboards and incident channels; collect SLO/latency regressions
Week 7: Post-canary tuning and prepare runtime-1.22 patch for broader rollout
risks_and_mitigation: Risk: Slab trimming could evict tokens that are immediately needed leading to recompute storms. Mitigation: pin most-recent-n slabs per prefix and only allow trimming of slabs older than observed reuse window; simulate with tracing to calibrate pin count.

Risk: Model swap compatibility issues (kv-format mismatch). Mitigation: enforce compatibility via small adapter layer that can translate or reject swap; maintain compatibility table in repo with test vectors.
Risk: Telemetry overload from per-slice traces. Mitigation: sample traces at 1% by default and enable full traces for failing requests during canary.
Risk: Increased CPU due to recomputation. Mitigation: measure CPU delta in staging and add backpressure to admission controller to prefer partial-response over heavy recompute.
Risk: Customer-visible partial responses reduce quality. Mitigation: only enable partial responses for low-impact customers or when SLA allows; product will own UX decisions for public rollout
tests: Unit: token-window slicing correctness for boundary conditions and overlapping requests
Unit: simulated slab reclaim frees expected bytes and respects pinning
Integration: multi-tenant continuous-batching test that reproduces previous OOM patterns and measures OOM reduction
Integration: compatibility smoke for each fallback micro-variant using a small corpus of eval prompts
E2E Canary: staged traffic with feature flag to trigger controller in 5% of requests; compare error rates/latency to control group
rollout_plan: Feature-flagged canary: 5% staging traffic for 48h with alerting on OOM_rate or latency regressions
Expand to 20% if metrics look stable for 72h, run full regression suite
If stable, promote to runtime-1.22 canary pool, collect 2 weeks of telemetry before broad rollout
Provide k-rollout knob to disable micro-evict in emergency
